subject: english-language

moments.title: The Language Instinct
moments.body: 1994: Pinker's 'The Language Instinct' published. The popular synthesis of Chomskyan generative linguistics with evolutionary psychology. Argument: language is an evolved cognitive capacity, not a cultural invention; UG is real; children acquire language because they are biologically equipped to.
moments.takeaway: Pinker's accessible writing reached audiences far beyond linguistics. The book made nativism the popular mainstream of language science.

moments.title: Words and Rules
moments.body: 1999: Pinker's 'Words and Rules' examines past tenses — both regular ('walked') and irregular ('went') — to argue for a dual-mechanism model. Rules generate regulars; words store irregulars. The framework became a standard reference in psycholinguistics.
moments.takeaway: Pinker's combination of empirical work and popular synthesis defined a generation of cognitive science writing.

moments.title: Debates and dissent
moments.body: Critics: Tomasello, Goldberg and others argue usage-based learning suffices without UG. Daniel Everett's work on Pirahã has been used to argue against language universals (controversial). The debate continues; most positions now accept some constraints and some learning.
moments.takeaway: Pinker's nativism remains influential but is not unchallenged. Modern child language research is more pluralistic.

now.title: Cognitive linguistics now
now.body: Modern cognitive linguistics includes generative grammar, usage-based approaches, neurolinguistics, evolutionary linguistics. Large language models (GPT et al.) raise new questions about how much innate structure language requires. Pinker himself has moved toward broader cognitive science popularisation.
now.open_questions: How much of language is innate? Modern consensus accepts that learning bias and architecture are needed; pure tabula rasa learning seems insufficient. The exact division remains contested.

reflection: A 1994 popular book defined how a generation thinks about language in cognitive science. Pinker's argument — that we have a language faculty as a biological inheritance — remains influential, and continues to be tested by new linguistic and computational evidence.
